Choose a basis for the first subspace of a flag, extend it to a basis for the second, and continue until obtaining a basis of the whole vector space. Do the same for the target flag. The unique linear map sending the first adapted basis to the second is invertible and sends every flagged subspace to its counterpart. Hence the action is transitive.

Yes. Let g send the first flag to the second and write d=detg=0. In an adapted basis of the target flag, scale its first vector by d−1 and fix the others. This defines a flag-preserving map h with determinant d−1. Then hg still sends the first flag to the second and has determinant one. Thus SL(n,K) is transitive as well.

B (Introduction to Fields)

Words: 250 Articles: 2
2008 OurBigBook.com

2

Words: 250 Articles: 1
B OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 250
2 OurBigBook.com
The characteristic is the smallest positive integer p with p1F​=0. Such an integer exists because the additive group is finite. If it factored as p=ab with 1<a,b<p, then (a1F​)(b1F​)=0 with both factors nonzero, contradicting the absence of zero divisors. Hence it is prime. The elements generated by 1F​ form a subfield isomorphic to Fp​. The finite set F is a finite-dimensional vector space of some dimension a≥1 over that subfield, so ∣F∣=pa​.
A nonzero polynomial of polynomial degree n over a field has at most n distinct roots. This follows by induction: a root r gives a factor X−r, and every different root must be a root of the remaining factor by cancellation. Thus Xn−1 has at most n roots. In the finite multiplicative group, the elements whose order divides n are exactly those satisfying xn=1. The supplied cyclicity criterion therefore proves that the multiplicative group is cyclic.
For the prime of the specified form write m=2rs with s odd. If s>1, then 22r+1 is a proper factor of (22r)s+1, impossible. Thus m is a power of two. Since 2m≡−1(modp), the order of two divides 2m but does not divide m. All divisors of the power of two 2m other than 2m itself divide m. Consequently
ordp​(2)=2m.​
(5)
It generates the multiplicative group precisely when 2m=p−1=2m. For positive integers m this holds exactly at m=1,2: from m=3 onward 2m>2m, and the inequality persists on increasing m. These give p=3 or 5​, equivalently the stated range among Fermat primes.

Solution

Words: 164
2 OurBigBook.com
The d distinct powers 1,a,…,ad−1 all satisfy Xd=1. The supplied root bound says they exhaust those roots. Thus every element of order d has the form an. If g=gcd(n,d), the least positive k with ank=1 is d/g, so
ordp​(an)=gcd(n,d)d​.​
(6)
This proves both directions of the first assertion.
For existence of a primitive root one may apply the finite-field cyclicity criterion proved in the preceding section. There is also a direct counting proof: for each divisor d of p−1, either no elements have order d, or the preceding argument shows there are exactly ϕ(d). Lagrange's theorem partitions all p−1 nonzero residue classes by such orders, while ∑d∣p−1​ϕ(d)=p−1. Every count is at most its corresponding ϕ(d), so equality of the totals forces equality at every divisor. In particular there are ϕ(p−1)​ primitive roots.
Put t=g(p−1)/8. It has order eight, so t4=−1 and t8=1. The specified element is k=t+t7=t+t−1. Since t−2=−t2, squaring gives k2=t2+2+t−2=2(modp)​.

On the product of two sigma-finite measure spaces, Tonelli's theorem states that a nonnegative measurable function has measurable iterated-integral functions and
∫X×Y​fd(μ×ν)=∫X​∫Y​fdνdμ=∫Y​∫X​fdμdν,
(13)
with values allowed to be infinite. Fubini's theorem states that if f is measurable and ∫X×Y​∣f∣<∞, then its sections are integrable almost everywhere, both iterated integrals exist as finite integrals, and the same equality holds, also for real or complex signed functions. Tonelli applied to ∣f∣ can first be used to verify the absolute-integrability hypothesis of Fubini.

because the quotient is bounded near zero. Fubini therefore permits reversing the order for this finite x interval. Direct integration in x yields

The distance function x↦d(x,c) is continuous because the triangle inequality gives ∣d(x,c)−d(y,c)∣≤d(x,y). Hence B(c,r)={x:d(x,c)≤r} is the inverse image of the closed interval (−∞,r], so is closed. Since it contains B(c,r), it also contains the closure of that open ball:
clB(c,r)⊆B(c,r).​

BE​=((0,1)×{0}),BE​=([0,1]×{0})∪({0}×[0,1/2]).​

a OurBigBook.com
A two-dimensional embedded submanifold is a subset which near every point can be straightened by a smooth local coordinate change in the ambient space to an open piece of the coordinate plane R2×{0}. Equivalently locally it has a regular smooth parametrization of rank two, with the induced local topology.
A tangent vector at x is the derivative γ′(0) of a smooth curve in the submanifold with γ(0)=x. These derivatives form the two-dimensional tangent space Tx​M. A normal vector is a vector orthogonal to every tangent vector. Its space is (Tx​M)⊥, which has dim(Tx​M)⊥=1​ in the three-dimensional ambient Euclidean space.

Nx​M=R(x1​/a2,x2​/b2,x3​/c2),​

Solution

Words: 335
2 OurBigBook.com
Assume the regular Sturm–Liouville setting: real coefficients with p>0, w>0 and sufficient continuity and differentiability for the integrations below. Apply a multiplier to J[y]−λ(∫ab​wy2−1). Its first variation in the direction η is
2[py′η]ab​−2∫ab​((py′)′+qy+λwy)ηdx.
(26)
Variations vanishing at both endpoints and the supplied fundamental lemma give
−(py′)′−qy=λwy.​
(27)
At a free endpoint the value of η is arbitrary, so the natural condition is py′=0 there. At a fixed endpoint η=0, so no such derivative condition is imposed; the prescribed endpoint value is imposed instead. This distinction also allows one endpoint of each type.
For eigenfunctions u,v of distinct eigenvalues λ,μ under the same homogeneous self-adjoint endpoint conditions, multiply their equations by v,u and subtract. Integration gives
(λ−μ)∫ab​wuvdx=[p(uv′−u′v)]ab​=0.
(28)
The boundary expression vanishes for both natural conditions and homogeneous fixed-value conditions. Thus ∫ab​wuv=0​ for different eigenvalues.
In the specified fixed-endpoint case the eigenproblem is −y′′−y=λy, y(0)=y(1)=0. There are no nonzero solutions when λ+1≤0; the elementary exponential or affine solutions and the two endpoint conditions prove this. For λ+1>0, the first condition leaves a sine and the second requires frequency nπ. The normalized stationary functions and eigenvalues are
yn​(x)=±2​sin(nπx),λn​=n2π2−1,n≥1.​
(29)
Distinct sine modes are orthogonal by the product-to-sum formula, or by the preceding Green second identity. Although they need not satisfy the natural derivative conditions, their fixed zero values also annihilate the boundary expression, so orthogonality is expected.
The Wirtinger inequality ∫01​y′2≥π2∫01​y2 gives J[y]≥π2−1. For completeness it follows by writing y=vsinπx for a smooth function supported away from the endpoints and integrating the cross term: ∫(y′2−π2y2)=∫sin2(πx)v′2≥0. Approximation extends it to the Dirichlet Sobolev class. Equality is attained by the first sine mode; the eigenproblem or equality condition gives only its scalar multiples. Hence the two normalized minimizers are y=±2​sinπx​ and the minimum is π2−1=λ1​​.
There is a wording distinction in the source: the two sign choices of the minimum are not orthogonal to each other, since their inner product is −1. Orthogonality applies to the stationary modes with different eigenvalues, not to both signs of the same minimizer.

The coordinate ψ is cyclic, so pψ​=C(ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ) is conserved. Initially the spin is zero, hence ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ=0​ throughout. The coordinate ϕ is also cyclic. After imposing this zero spin, its conserved momentum becomes (A+mh2)ϕ˙​sin2θ. Initially θ=π/2 and ϕ˙​=ω, so ϕ˙​sin2θ=ω​.
The equation for z is
dtd​[m(z˙−hsinθθ˙)]=−mg.

The quantity in parentheses is the vertical velocity of the centre of mass. Initially that velocity and its height are both zero: the initial rotation is horizontal and the vertex starts at rest at the reference height. Twice integrating gives
z+hcosθ=−21​gt2.​
(36)
Independently, the frictionless vertical wire exerts only horizontal force. Gravity is therefore the only vertical external force on the body, and the centre of mass undergoes vertical free fall. This gives the same equation without the angular equations.

In vacuum the source-free equations are
∇⋅E=∇⋅B=0,∇×E=−Bt​,∇×B=c−2Et​.
(37)
Adding the divergence equations with weights 1,ic gives the complex divergence equation. Adding the curl equations in the same way gives ∇×W=(i/c)Wt​. Conversely real and imaginary parts of these two complex equations recover all four real equations.
For the cosine ansatz, differentiation yields divergence (Ω⋅K)sin(ωt−K⋅x) and curl −(Ω×K)sin(ωt−K⋅x). The time derivative is −ωΩsin(ωt−K⋅x). Since that sine is not identically zero, the required conditions are precisely
Ω⋅K=0,Ω×K=(iω/c)Ω.​
(38)
Dotting the second equation with Ω gives Ω⋅Ω=0 because ω=0. This dot product is complex bilinear, not Hermitian. Taking the cross product again with K and using transversality gives −∣K∣2Ω=−ω2Ω/c2. Nonzero amplitude therefore requires ∣K∣2=ω2/c2​.
Taking real and imaginary parts yields the full conditions
e⋅K=b⋅K=0,K×e=ωb,b×K=(ω/c2)e.​
(39)
They imply e⋅b=0 and ∣e∣=c∣b∣, together with the dispersion relation. Conversely a nonzero transverse e, this dispersion relation and b=K×e/ω satisfy all the conditions.
The physical fields are E=ecos(ωt−K⋅x) and B=bcos(ωt−K⋅x). Each oscillates along one fixed real direction, so both fields are linearly polarized. Complex encoding of the two fields here does not mean either real field is circularly polarized.

F(z)=f(z)+f(a2/zˉ)​.

On ∣z∣=a, the relation a2/zˉ=z makes F=f+fˉ​ real. Thus its imaginary part, the stream function, is constant on the circle and the normal velocity vanishes. This proves the theorem, with any harmless additive constant left free. Its usual decay condition at infinity selects the surrounding flow inherited from f.
Write a1​=z1​ for the dipole position to distinguish it from the circle radius, now one. Substitution gives

The image singularity is at 1/aˉ1​, strictly inside the solid circle. This exterior potential has the original dipole and an impermeable cylinder boundary.

The moment generating function is MX​(t)=E(etX) wherever that expectation is finite. A useful continuity theorem says that if the moment generating functions Mn​ are finite on a common open interval containing zero and converge pointwise there to the moment generating function of a probability distribution, then the corresponding variables converge in distribution to that law. Equivalently one may assume a finite limiting function on such a neighborhood, with the usual continuity at zero, and obtain the uniquely determined limiting law.
For the gamma density, integrating the exponential against the density and changing variable to (λ−t)x gives
MX​(t)=(λ−tλ​)α,t<λ.​

For the waiting time to one head, independence of successive tosses gives Pr(Y=j)=p(1−p)j−1 for j≥1. Summing the geometric series gives
MY​(t)=1−(1−p)etpet​,(1−p)et<1.​
(51)
The waiting times between consecutive heads are independent copies of Y, so their sum N has moment generating function MY​(t)k. Consequently
M2pN​(t)=[1−(1−p)e2ptpe2pt​]k⟶(1−2t)−k.

For fixed t<1/2, numerator and denominator have leading terms p and p(1−2t) as p↓0. A fixed neighborhood of zero is inside the convergence domain for all sufficiently small p, so the continuity theorem applies. The limiting distribution is

A state is recurrent if, starting there, the probability of returning at some strictly positive time is one. It is transient if that return probability is strictly less than one. Suppose i,j communicate. Choose r,s with pji​(r)>0 and pij​(s)>0. Chapman–Kolmogorov gives
pjj​(r+n+s)≥pji​(r)pii​(n)pij​(s).
(55)
If i is recurrent, summing over n and using the supplied return-series criterion makes the return series for j diverge, so j is recurrent. Interchanging the states proves equivalence; therefore transience is also constant on a communicating class.
For the nearest-neighbor walk, return in an odd number of steps is impossible. A return in 2n steps requires exactly n steps each way, so
pii​(2n)=(n2n​)[p(1−p)]n∼πn​[4p(1−p)]n​.
(56)
At p=1/2, the return series diverges like ∑n−1/2. If 0<p<1 and p=1/2, then 4p(1−p)<1, so it converges by exponential decay. At p=0 or one the walk never returns. Hence recurrence occurs exactly at p=1/2​.

This does not establish equality of the means; it states that the observed difference does not cross this test's two-sided threshold.
Age matching introduces a shared block factor: the two observations in a pair can be associated, and their age-dependent means also undermine the simple unblocked independent-samples model. A paired t-test on the within-pair drug-minus-placebo differences accounts for that design, assuming independent pairs and the corresponding normal-difference model. Shared age variation cancels in those differences; positive within-pair association reduces their variance and can increase power, although the reduction in degrees of freedom means improvement is not automatic. The paired test cannot be computed from the two marginal means and variances alone: the within-pair differences or covariance are needed.

a OurBigBook.com
For a finite graph choose a simple path of maximum length. Every neighbor of its final vertex must already lie on the path, since otherwise that vertex could be appended. The final vertex has degree at least two, so besides its predecessor it has another neighbor earlier on the path. That edge together with the intervening path segment makes a cycle in a graph.
Finiteness is needed for this assertion in general: the two-sided infinite path has degree two at every vertex and no cycle in a graph. The customary finite-graph convention is used here and in the subsequent cube questions.
b
Words: 178 Articles: 1
i OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 178
b OurBigBook.com
For a closed Eulerian trail, every visit to a vertex pairs one entering edge with one departing edge, including the initial/final vertex. Thus every degree is even.
Conversely, in a finite connected graph with all degrees even, start at a vertex and follow unused edges until no extension is possible. The walk cannot stop away from its starting point: at a different endpoint an odd number of its incident edges would have been used, leaving at least one unused edge because its total degree is even. Thus it closes. If any edge remains unused, connectedness gives a vertex of the current closed trail incident with an unused edge. Repeat the construction from that vertex in the unused-edge subgraph and splice the resulting closed trail into the first one. Finitely many edges make the procedure terminate in a closed trail using every edge exactly once.
Hence a connected finite graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when all degrees are even. If “trail” is allowed to be open, the printed equivalence needs correction: a connected graph has an Eulerian trail when it has zero or two odd-degree vertices. A single edge is an immediate counterexample to the unqualified printed statement.

Solution
Words: 113
a OurBigBook.com
Assume the fixed margins are compatible, so the finite state space is nonempty. At state X, draw an index table Y from the stipulated uniform proposal law. If X+Y has any negative entry, reject and stay at X; otherwise accept and set the next state to X+Y. The margins stay fixed because the proposal has zero row and column sums.
The proposal set is invariant under Y↦−Y. Hence proposals between two feasible distinct states are symmetric. The target density is constant, so the Metropolis–Hastings acceptance probability for a feasible proposal is one. The explicit rejection of infeasible proposals is essential: fixed margins by themselves do not guarantee nonnegative entries.

Solution
Words: 64
b OurBigBook.com
Let L be the number of index tables, including the zero table. If distinct feasible states A,B differ by an index table, then P(A,B)=1/L=P(B,A), using the sign-reversal bijection for the reverse move. If they do not differ by an index table, both probabilities are zero. Since π is uniform,
π(A)P(A,B)=π(B)P(B,A).​
(76)
For equal states detailed balance is tautological. Thus the chain is reversible and its uniform distribution is stationary.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
A finite irreducible aperiodic Markov chain converges to its unique stationary distribution from every initial state. Finiteness holds because nonnegative entries with fixed finite row sums are bounded. The given connecting-sequence property makes the chain irreducible: each feasible step in such a sequence has positive proposal probability and is accepted. The all-zero index table occurs with probability 1/L>0 and gives a self-loop at every state, establishing aperiodicity. Reversibility supplied the stationary uniform law in (b). Consequently
Pr(Xt​=x)⟶π(x)for every state x.​
(77)
The conclusion also holds when the feasible state space is a singleton.

i OurBigBook.com
A mixed strategy for Player II is a probability vector q≥0 with ∑j​qj​=1, specifying the random choice of a column. If Player I chooses row i, the expected payment is (Aq)i​. A mixture of rows cannot exceed the maximum of these row expectations, so the smallest payment Player II can guarantee is
v=q≥0, 1Tq=1min​imax​(Aq)i​.​
(78)
An optimal strategy is a vector attaining that minimum, which exists by compactness of the probability simplex and continuity. The minimax theorem identifies this guaranteed loss with Player I's maximal guaranteed gain, the value of the finite zero-sum game.

Strictly positive entries imply v>0. If q is an optimal strategy, set x=q/v. Then Ax≤1 and 1Tx=1/v. Conversely, a nonzero feasible x with s=1Tx gives a strategy q=x/s satisfying maxi​(Aq)i​≤1/s. Thus v≤1/s, or s≤1/v. The optimal objective is therefore s∗​=1/v, and
v=1/s∗​,q∗​=x∗​/s∗​.​
(79)
A nonzero feasible point exists by taking a sufficiently small positive multiple of a probability vector, and positivity of A bounds the feasible objective, so the optimum is attained.
For general entries choose a constant c so that A′=A+c11T is strictly positive. Every pair of strategies has its payoff increased by exactly c, so optimal strategies are unchanged. Solve the positive problem for A′, recover v′=1/s∗′​, and then v=v′−c​ for the original game.

Its expected payoff against every column is at least v. Thus the primal represents Player II's minimization of worst loss and the dual represents Player I's maximization of guaranteed gain.

Both objectives equal 1/4: 1Tx=1/12+1/6=1/4 and 1Ty=1/6+1/12=1/4. Weak duality bounds the value of every primal feasible point above by every dual feasible objective. Equality for this feasible pair therefore proves both are optimal, without needing to solve either problem further.

p=(2/3,1/3),q=(1/3,0,2/3),v=4.​

As a direct check Aq=(4,4)T and pTA=(4,5,4), so Player II guarantees a loss of at most four and Player I guarantees a gain of at least four.
